blogs.title: Commissioner-Only Penalties under Minnesota’s MPWA: The Eighth Circuit Reads § 181.101 Narrowly
blogs.description: The court held that average daily wage penalties under Minn. Stat. § 181.101 can be sought only by the Commissioner, not by private plaintiffs. This post unpacks the text-first analysis, contrasts § 181.101 with employee-empowering penalty provisions in §§ 181.13 and 181.14, and situates the ruling alongside Hull v. ConvergeOne. We’ll explore practical implications for wage plaintiffs who have been paid their wages but want leverage via penalties, what this means for settlement dynamics, and whether a legislative fix is likely or advisable.

blogs.title: MFLSA Penalties Meet Article III: Tender, Voluntary Cessation, and the Laidlaw Question
blogs.description: Although the employer paid all overtime and liquidated damages, the Eighth Circuit vacated summary judgment on MFLSA penalties and remanded for a jurisdictional inquiry. This post examines the standing and mootness tension: when do statutory penalties payable to the state still redress a private plaintiff’s injury under Friends of the Earth v. Laidlaw? We analyze the remand’s focus on whether the challenged overtime policy persists, the role of voluntary cessation, and Judge Kobes’s separate doubts about standing. We also consider strategic takeaways for defendants who tender wages mid-suit and for plaintiffs pressing class claims when penalties are government-directed.

blogs.title: The Vanishing MWTA Claim: Notice Violations, Penalties, and Waiver on Appeal
blogs.description: Cohen’s Minnesota Wage Theft Act claim—premised on failure to give notice of an overtime policy change—fell because he stipulated to receiving all owed wages and failed to identify any statutory authority for private penalties. This post surveys § 181.032’s remedial structure, why the absence of a clearly authorized civil penalty is dispositive, and how appellate waiver (failure to brief with authority) doomed the claim. We also outline compliance lessons for employers about documenting policy changes and notice, even as the opinion signals limited private penalty exposure under the MWTA for such violations.

blogs.title: Remedies Must Be Pleaded: Injunctive Relief, Rule 15, and the Late Pivot Problem
blogs.description: The panel refused to consider a new request to rescind the 2019 overtime policy raised for the first time at summary judgment, reiterating that new claims and forms of relief belong in amended complaints under Rule 15. This post offers pleading and motion-practice guidance for wage-and-hour litigants seeking prospective relief, including timing, evidentiary needs, and coordination with penalty theories. We also flag Judge Kobes’s separate note on attorney’s fees, costs, and prejudgment interest—issues likely to surface on remand if jurisdiction persists—and discuss how fee entitlement can hinge on securing non-moot relief.
